lines: Why can a model ace training, then fail on new data?

lines.text: Because it memorized. It didn't learn.

scenes.label: THE PROBLEM
lines: We train a model on examples, then use it on data it has never seen.
This model passes through every training point.
But real data has noise.
On new points, its predictions are way off.

scenes.label: THE IDEA
lines: That's overfitting: the model learns the noise, not the pattern.
Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple to catch the pattern.
We want the fit in between.

scenes.label: HOW IT WORKS
lines: Plot error against model complexity.
Training error keeps falling as the model grows.
Validation error falls too, then turns back up.
On the left, both are high: underfitting, or high bias.
On the right, the gap widens: overfitting, or high variance.
The sweet spot is where validation error is lowest.

scenes.label: IN PRODUCTION
lines: Say we train a fraud detector on card payments.
Every epoch, the training loss goes down.
Validation loss drops, then starts climbing after epoch twelve.
Early stopping keeps the model from its best epoch.

scenes.label: BEFORE vs AFTER
lines: An overfit model looks perfect in training, then fails on real users.
A well fit model is validated, regularized, and stopped early, so it generalizes.

scenes.label: INTERVIEW NOTES
lines: Remember three things.

lines.text: 1. Underfitting is high bias: bad on training and on new data.
lines.say: One. Underfitting is high bias: bad on training, and on new data.

lines.text: 2. Overfitting is high variance: great on training, bad on new data.
lines.say: Two. Overfitting is high variance: great on training, bad on new data.

lines.text: 3. Fight overfitting with more data, regularization, dropout, or early stopping.
lines.say: Three. Fight overfitting with more data, regularization, dropout, or early stopping.

lines.text: A good model learns the pattern, not the noise.
